records.value:
• Critical Thinking and Problem Solving: the learner uses a cylinder and a cone of the same radius and height, and a substance such as sand or water, to determine the volume of a cone as a third of the volume of a cylinder. In this unit learners also the learner analyses composite solid shapes found in real-life Kenyan contexts — such as grain silos in Eldoret or water tanks in rural Rift Valley — and decomposes them to determine total surface area and volume.
• Creativity and Imagination: the learner uses a cylinder and a cone of the same radius and height, and a substance such as sand or water, to determine the volume of a cone as a third the volume of a cylinder. In this unit learners also improvises and constructs nets and models of prisms, pyramids, cones and spheres using locally available materials (cardboard, manila paper) to verify surface area formulae.
• Also practised in this unit (not named in the KICD design for this sub-strand):
• Communication and Collaboration: the learner discusses and shares findings with peers when measuring and calculating the surface area and volume of locally available solid models such as tins, packets and containers used for ugali flour or cooking oil.
• Digital Literacy: the learner uses digital devices and software (where available) to explore 3D solid models, nets and volume visualisations.
• Self-Efficacy: the learner builds confidence in applying surface area and volume formulae independently to solve real-world packaging, construction and storage problems relevant to Kenyan industries.

records.value:
• Unity: the learner discusses in a group and establishes the relationship between the volume of a cone and the volume of a cylinder. In this unit learners also works collaboratively in groups to construct solid models, measure dimensions and verify calculated surface areas and volumes, appreciating each member's contribution.
• Respect: the learner listens to others' opinions as they discuss in groups and work out the volumes of prisms, pyramids, cones, frustums and spheres. In this unit learners also recognises and values the input of every group member during practical activities involving the construction and measurement of solid models.
• Also practised in this unit (not named in the KICD design for this sub-strand):
• Responsibility: the learner carefully handles models of solids and measurement tools collected from the immediate environment, and accurately records measurements to ensure correct calculations of surface area and volume.
• Integrity: the learner applies formulae with accurate measurements and honest working, adhering to mathematical rigour when solving surface area and volume problems.

records.value:
• Environment and technology: as the learner collects and uses containers from the immediate environment and uses them to discuss and work out their volumes.
• Also linked in this unit (not named in the KICD design for this sub-strand):
• Education for Sustainable Development (Environmental Education): the learner uses and repurposes locally available materials such as cardboard packaging, tin cans and plastic containers to construct solid models, promoting environmental consciousness and waste reduction.
• Social Cohesion: the learner works in groups to build models, measure solids and solve problems, fostering teamwork and mutual respect across diverse learner backgrounds.
• Socio-Economic Issues: the learner applies surface area and volume concepts to real Kenyan economic contexts such as determining the amount of metal sheet needed to fabricate a water tank in Nakuru, or the capacity of a grain store in the Rift Valley, linking mathematics to livelihoods and national development.
• Home Science and Technology: the learner connects volume calculations to everyday household decisions such as estimating the volume of a sufuria used for cooking ugali or the capacity of a storage jerrycan.

records.old: A sphere is best of all, so artisans choose
records.new: A sphere is best of all: made into a sphere, the same 30,800 cm2 of sheet would have r = 49.5 cm (4 x 22/7 x r2 = 30,800 gives r2 = 2,450) and hold about 508 litres (4/3 x 22/7 x r3), more than the drum's 404.25 litres. Even so, artisans choose
records.group_headline: 'A sphere is best of all' and the Lesson 8 sphere prediction were never tested; now checked with numbers (30,800 cm2 as a sphere holds about 508 litres)
records.why: The unit repeatedly says a sphere is best of all and Lesson 8 asks learners to predict it, but nobody ever calculates it, and Lesson 6 calls it 'established'. Checked twice: 4 x 22/7 x r2 = 30,800 gives r2 = 30,800 x 7 / 88 = 2,450, r = 49.497 cm; V = 4/3 x 22/7 x 49.497^3 = 508,174 cm3 (508 litres); using exact pi the answer is 508,276 cm3, so 'about 508 litres' holds. 508 > 404.25 litres, so the claim is true for these numbers.
records.reference: Isoperimetric inequality for solids: among all solids with a given surface area the sphere has the greatest volume (e.g. Courant and Robbins, What Is Mathematics?, chapter on maxima and minima)

records.old: Ask: 'A sphere is best of all, so why does Wanjiru not make spherical tanks for grain?'
records.new: First test the Predict-phase sphere prediction with the class: 'If Wanjiru bends 30,800 cm2 of sheet into a sphere, what is r, and what does it hold?' (4 x 22/7 x r2 = 30,800, so r2 = 2,450 and r is about 49.5 cm; V = 4/3 x 22/7 x r3 is about 508,000 cm3, about 508 litres, more than the drum's 404.25 litres.) Then ask: 'A sphere is best of all, so why does Wanjiru not make spherical tanks for grain?'
records.why: Knock-on edit of the sphere test: gives teachers the worked check and the expected numbers.
records.reference: Isoperimetric inequality for solids (sphere has the greatest volume for a given surface area); see group root.

records.old: Use only the established idea that a sphere is best of all for a fixed surface area, without deriving it.
records.new: Tell learners that, for a fixed surface area, the sphere holds the most (a known mathematical result); they will test it with numbers in Lesson 8, so do not derive it now.
records.why: Lesson 6 called the sphere result 'established' although nothing in the unit had shown it. It is now told as a fact to be tested in Lesson 8.

records.old: toward 'a sphere covers the most space for its skin'
records.new: and sets up the Lesson 8 test of whether a sphere holds more than the drum for the same sheet
records.why: Lesson 4 only finds surface areas; it does not show that a sphere holds the most. The purpose now says what it really sets up.

records.old: A sphere is the best of all, since it encloses the most space for the least covering.
records.new: A sphere is the best of all, since it encloses the most space for the least covering: 30,800 cm2 of sheet made into a sphere has r = 49.5 cm and holds about 508 litres, more than the drum's 404.25 litres.
records.why: Knock-on edit of the sphere test: gives teachers the worked check and the expected numbers.
records.reference: Isoperimetric inequality for solids; see group root.

value.criterion: Calculating surface area and volume correctly
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Uses the correct method for each solid (prism, cylinder, pyramid, cone, sphere, composite), uses slant height and vertical height correctly, gets all values right (30,800 cm2; 404,250 cm3; 322,500 cm3) with correct units and working.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Uses mostly correct methods and gets most values right, with one or two small slips in arithmetic, units or choice of height.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Confuses formulae, mixes slant and vertical height, or omits working and units, so the values are mostly incorrect.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: States clearly that surface area is the material covering a solid and volume is the space inside, and correctly classifies each task as a surface area or volume question with reasons.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Distinguishes the two ideas correctly but gives limited reasons or misclassifies one task.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Treats surface area and volume as the same thing or cannot say which one a task needs.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Explains why the drum holds 81.75 litres more than the box using the shared 30,800 cm2, both volumes and the cross-section areas (3,850 cm2 against 2,500 cm2), noting that the drum's larger base outweighs the box's extra height, and links to the sphere as the most efficient shape.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Explains that shape decides capacity and quotes the main numbers, but the reasoning about cross-sections is incomplete.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: States that the drum holds more without evidence, or suggests that equal surface area means equal volume.

value.criterion: Handling composite solids and real-life application
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Leaves out hidden joined faces in surface area, adds the volumes of the parts, and describes a realistic Kenyan design, explaining which calculation gives sheet and which gives capacity, plus a relevant career.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Handles composite solids mostly correctly and gives a reasonable Kenyan application with some detail missing.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Counts hidden faces or gives no clear real-life application.

records.why: The CBE rubric has four levels (Exceeds, Meets, Approaches, Below Expectations) but the current data contract allows only three level fields, so Below Expectations cannot be written. Suggestion: teachers treat work that does not reach 'Approaches Expectations' as Below Expectations until the contract allows a fourth field.

records.old: Draw the table on the board and fill it with learners' values.
records.new: Draw the table on the board and fill it with learners' values. Language and access support: start a unit word wall with a sketch and an English and Kiswahili label for each key term: surface area (eneo la uso), volume (ujazo), prism (prisma), pyramid (piramidi), cone (koni), sphere (tufe), base (msingi), height (urefu). Ask Kiswahili speakers to confirm or correct the terms, let learners explain in Kiswahili first if that helps, and keep the wall up for all eight lessons. For learners who find cutting or writing hard, give pre-made nets and tactile models, let a partner record, and accept an oral or drawn answer instead of a written one.
records.why: The unit had no language support for English learners and no accommodations for learners with special needs. This adds a short word wall (teacher decision: I could not verify the Kiswahili terms, so teachers should confirm them with a Kiswahili colleague) and ways to take part and show understanding other than cutting and writing.

records.old: total surface area, volume, capacity, Driving Question Board
records.new: total surface area, Driving Question Board
records.why: Lesson 1 is only about surface area; volume and capacity are Lessons 5 and 6. The keywords feed the resource matcher, and these two could bring up a volume video that spoils the later discovery.
records.group_headline: Resource search words for Lessons 1 and 2 could pull in volume or curved-surface resources before those ideas are taught; removed

records.old: total surface area, curved surface, Wanjiru
records.new: total surface area, Wanjiru
records.why: A pyramid has no curved surface; 'curved surface' could bring in cone resources before Lesson 3.

records.old: Scissors and craft knives: cut away from the body and keep fingers clear of the blade.
records.new: Scissors only: cut away from the body and keep fingers clear of the blades. Do not use craft knives or other blades in class.
records.why: Craft knives were allowed here although Lesson 1 forbids blades; card nets cut safely with blunt-tipped scissors.

records.old: For learners who struggle, offer a pre-labelled diagram and the formula card from Lesson 3.
records.new: For learners who struggle, offer a pre-labelled diagram and the formula card from Lesson 3. If footballs are short, share one per station and rotate, or use any round ball (a netball, a tennis ball, or crumpled paper wrapped in masking tape): measure its circumference and find its r first, then use that r. At Station B, if learners do not recall 2πrh, unroll a card cylinder: the curved wall is a rectangle with length 2πr (the circumference) and width h, the same idea as perimeter x length in Lesson 1.
records.why: Two gaps for large classes: footballs are scarce (low-cost substitute added), and the cylinder wall formula 2πrh is used for the container and the drum but never shown. Linking it to the Lesson 1 prism idea makes it follow from what learners know.

records.old: Level the sand at the rim; do not heap it.
records.new: Level the sand at the rim; do not heap it. (Teacher preparation: make the models beforehand from card and tape, with the pyramid and prism sharing the same base and the same vertical height; dry sand, rice or maize is easier to pour than water in card models.)
records.why: Low-cost way to make and use the models in schools without ready-made hollow solids.

records.old: Insist on 'level to the brim' and 'no spills'.
records.new: Insist on 'level to the brim' and 'no spills'. If ready-made hollow models are not available, roll card into a cylinder (r = 7 cm, h = 12 cm) and make the cone from a card sector of radius about 13.9 cm (the slant height) and angle about 181 degrees, tape the seams, and use dry sand, rice or maize instead of water.
records.why: Low-cost substitute for hollow cone and cylinder models. Checked: l = square root of (7 x 7 + 12 x 12) = square root of 193, about 13.9 cm; sector angle = 360 x r / l = 360 x 7 / 13.9, about 181 degrees.

Lesson 3 adds up to 40 minutes (6 + 12 + 10 + 6 + 6) but holds the cone net, the sector derivation, the frustum and three calculation tasks with shared scissors and string. The lesson already allows a double period. Suggestion: plan 80 minutes if your class is large, and keep the 40-minute plan only if the cones are pre-cut. Phase times are left unchanged.

records.old: Do not rush this algebra: allow 15 seconds wait before asking, 'Why does the answer match?'
records.new: Do not rush this algebra: allow 15 seconds wait before asking, 'Why does the answer match?' Tell learners honestly that this shows the formula working for the Turkana tank; the general proof uses similar triangles (r/R = small slant / big slant) and is not needed in Grade 10.
records.why: The halving trick works because the two cones are exactly half-size; it is a check for this tank, not a proof of the general formula. A teacher should not present it as a full derivation.

records.old: choose between a conical, cylindrical and hemispherical roof-catchment tank; all use the same amount of plastic sheeting — students investigate which shape stores the most water, exploring volume and surface area of cones, cylinders and spheres
records.new: choose between a frustum-shaped (a cone with its top cut off), cylindrical and hemispherical water tank; all use the same amount of sheet — students investigate which shape stores the most water, exploring volume and surface area of frustums, cylinders and spheres
records.why: The lessons use a frustum-shaped Turkana tank (Lessons 3 and 6), not a conical roof-catchment tank, so the supporting phenomenon now matches what learners actually calculate.

records.old: Tell groups to bring dimensions and a community need for Lesson 8.
records.new: Set the Lesson 8 project as homework: each group chooses a community need (grain silo, water tank or sufuria), fixes its dimensions, and calculates the total surface area of material and the capacity in litres, ready to present.
records.why: Lesson 8 expects finished designs with TSA and capacity, but nothing gave learners time or a clear task to do the calculations before it.

records.old: Groups give 4-minute project presentations (grain silo for a cooperative in Nakuru or Uasin Gishu, water tank for a Turkana or Kajiado community, or a sufuria for a school kitchen), followed by 2 minutes of critique.
records.new: (About 36 minutes.) Groups give 3-minute project presentations (grain silo for a cooperative in Nakuru or Uasin Gishu, water tank for a Turkana or Kajiado community, or a sufuria for a school kitchen), followed by 1 minute of critique.
records.why: In a class of 40 with about 10 groups, 4 + 2 minutes each takes 60 minutes, so with the other four phases (about 8 + 14 + 8 + 14 = 44) the lesson needed about 104 minutes. At 3 + 1 minutes (9 groups = 36 minutes) the total is 8 + 36 + 14 + 8 + 14 = 80.
records.group_headline: Lesson 8 presentations alone needed about 60 of the 80 minutes; shortened to 3 + 1 minutes per group (about 36 minutes in total)

records.old: Run a timer.
records.new: Run a timer: 3 minutes to present and 1 minute to critique. With more than 9 groups, run two gallery spaces or let some groups present on posters.
records.why: Knock-on edit of the shorter presentation time, with a plan for larger classes.

records.old: count how many circles' worth are used (about 4). Record: strip area ÷ circle area.
records.new: count how many circles' worth the half ball used (about 2) and double it for the whole ball (about 4). Record: whole-ball strip area ÷ circle area.
records.why: The text had learners cover only half the ball but expect about 4 circles' worth. Half a sphere is 2 great circles' worth (half of 4 x 346.5 = 693 cm2); doubling gives 4. Checked: 4 x 346.5 = 1,386 cm2 = 4 x 22/7 x 10.5 x 10.5.
records.group_headline: Football strip activity: covering half the ball cannot give 'about 4 circles'; learners now double the half-ball result
records.reference: Archimedes, On the Sphere and Cylinder (surface of a sphere = four great circles); KICD Grade 10 curriculum design, Mathematics, 2.7 (use of models)

records.old: (accept 3.8 to 4.2)
records.new: (accept 3.5 to 4.5)
records.why: Hands-on strip wrapping on a curved ball leaves gaps and overlaps, so 3.8 to 4.2 is too tight; the teacher moves already expect groups near 4 and a re-check for 3 or 5.
records.reference: Archimedes, On the Sphere and Cylinder; see group root.
